posts.text: At the start of the year, I finished a digital MOC of the Stinger Mantis from the Jedi series at lego's flagship scale and trying to largely keep their design schemes in mind. Since then I've been making slow bricklink orders to piece it together, and last week after some overtime I finally pulled the trigger on the remaining parts I needed (mainly some comparatively expensive slopes) The main goal I was trying to accomplish with this to incorporate the two separately rotating wings- using ratchet joints, the main wing rotates around the body, and the smaller wing with engine rotates separately with the ability to lock into place in the flight and landing orientations. You can see that it can sit in landing position without the stand- there's a slight tilt, so I may try to work landing gear for the outrigger engine into the V2. The mantis's unique cockpit shape is hard to accomplish with real bricks, but some panels make it so you can see out the front. Here's a shot showing how many figures you can fit in the interior- the only purist custom I have from fallen order is Cal, so I filled it out with pilots A better look at the interior- it was important to me to fit in the two-wide cockpit with comms station just behind. Past that we have the mission select table, living area with couch and table, and a very small representation of the kitchen. There's also a tiny version of the plant setup that's not very visible here but is signified by that yellow stripe on the back opposite the couch. For scaling, here it is alongside the 2019 Falcon. posts.title: [MOD] Blacktron Battrax upgrades
posts.text: Since my Monorail upgrades won't be built in the near future, I decided to shift my focus to smaller vehicles first. First up is 6941 Battrax. The Battrax was an amazing vehicle that I couldn't appreciate as a kid (because I was as spaceship crazy as Benny). I love it now, but it still has plenty of things that always annoyed me. So it was time to give it some upgrades. Cockpit The cockpit always was a major point of annoyance to me, for 2 reasons. First, why extending the canopy if not using the extra space? Second, why are there so many openings? Front sides are wide open, preventing storage of anything in front of the driver. Even the floor has an opening right behind the driver. So I decided to rebuild the cockpit entirely. The original driver position has been moved 1 stud back, keeping its original controller tile for a navigator/operator co-pilot. In front of him sits the actual driver, with a steering wheel and his own control panel. All the holes are closed, so they can save their oxygen! Lastly, I got rid of the yellow base plate underneath that felt totally out of place when viewed from underneath. As a finishing touch, added an inverted curved slope to extend it smoothly to the nose. Wheels I never questioned the wheels at first. Until I set up a chase with the Space Police Spy-Trak I in pursuit. The Battrax wheels suddenly felt rather small. So I test fitted the Spy-Trak wheels on the Battrax (not the first person to do this), and that fits well after moving the rear axle 1 stud back. But those wheels didn't look right either. The Battrax looked faster, and those big wide balloon tires feel like a better fit on industrial vehicles that literally crawl forward. So I started looking at more modern tires and settled for a fairly new 55.9x22 model. This works for me! Flight unit controls Remember how the box and manual show the astronaut flying the top rear section without the cockpit attached? And yet, not a single button or lever is present at this seat! So I've replaced the longer slopes by shorter grille slopes, and added control levers for the pilot. Other stuff Replaced most of the printed grille bricks and tiles by moulded ones. Replaced the old hoses by thicker modern ones. This is yet to be tested in bricks when the parts arrive. If the new ones are too stiff and keep pulling the headlight bricks off I might revert back to the old hoses. At the bottom rear, I gave the base plate the same inverted curved slope finish as I did in the front.

posts.title: So, what Do people want?
posts.text: I doubt it is that it is too expensive to make it profitable but more that there is not the market to make it worthwhile or profitable no matter what the cost is. 9V has been gone 15 years, to expect a company to keep making adapters as they change their products is unrealistic. They are also simple electronics and enthusiastic fans (especially fans of vintage items that are used to repairing) will typically make them, and so LEGO probably knows that even if they made a 9V-PUp converter (and a separate PF converter and a separate 12V converter), then fans would still make their own cheaper bespoke versions that do exactly what they want them to do. It is understandable that LEGO wants all of the electronic products that are available at one time are compatible but not necessarily compatible with products with those from over a decade before. What I'd prefer to see is a guarantee from LEGO that they will support a system until a specific date, so that you will always be able to buy components for that system until that date and if a new system is introduced in that time then compatability adapters will be available. That way, a buyer knows that their (probably expensive) product will have official support and compatability for a given time and may well put off investing in items if close to the end or buy plenty of spares if they are nearing the end of support date. A lot of my kit is PF and although I bought plenty of spare official motors when they were nearing the end, the extension cables sold out quickly and weren’t restocked. If I had known that, I would probably have bought more for cutting and modifying. Even used connectors are getting expensive now that I tend to attach small banana plugs to official connectors rather than hard wiring a motor to a connector, so I can easily swap out the (unofficial) motor if I want to change it. I also find now buying old IR receivers can be cheaper than official connectors!
